about: QR code: how a torn QR code still scans. How tech works, part 4. Puzzle film built on a real, tested object: this torn QR code still scans. Why: part of every QR code is backup, Reed-Solomon error correction (the same math music CDs use, per Denso Wave). At its top level, H, about 30% of its codewords (8-bit bytes) can be restored (Denso Wave, ISO/IEC 18004 outline spec). But only if the three corner squares survive: the position detection patterns tell the camera where the code is and, from any angle, which way is up. Denso Wave's team picked their 1:1:3:1:1 pattern after surveying fliers, magazines and cardboard boxes for the rarest one. Announced in 1994 by Denso Wave, then part of car-parts maker DENSO, for factory use where codes get dirty. Its maker says level M (about 15%) is the one most often picked. Ends asking the viewer to find a QR code and say which corner is empty. Factory #9. Narration-led: the voice is recorded first and every visual beat is keyed to its word times.
